title: Acadia NP
paragraphs: Acadia's coast steps down to the sea in great blocks of pink granite, with the Atlantic waiting at the bottom. Bar Harbor was the last port of call on my Canada and New England cruise and the gateway to Acadia National Park, which fills much of Mount Desert Island (pronounced like dessert, not the Sahara!). Samuel de Champlain gave the island that name back in 1604, for its bare mountaintops. The ship anchored out in Frenchman Bay, a tender ferried me ashore, and I had one clear blue day to see as much of the island as I could.

Start with the rock. Acadia's granite formed as molten rock that hardened far below the surface, and glaciers later ground the mountains down into the rounded shapes you see today. Now the ocean takes its turn. Spruce trees cling to the ledges right down to the waterline while the surf pounds away below them. At Thunder Hole, the sea squeezes into a narrow chasm and surges back out in a rush of white foam. It is named for the boom the waves make when they slam in, and it puts on its best show on a rising tide, so plan around the tides. Watch that much water hit that much rock and you feel a little temporary.

Inland, everything slows down. Jordan Pond is so clear you can see the stones on its bottom. At the far end sit the Bubbles, two round granite mountains that look about as threatening as their name, with a pair of round clouds floating above them as if to match. Late that afternoon a tender carried me back out to the ship. The cruise ended in Boston the next day, and by sunset I was on a plane home, watching the clouds turn the same pink as the granite.
